1.title: The keeper of their story

p.3: In many countries, the child legally becomes an adult. But a life doesn’t suddenly change on the day of a birthday.
p.4: What may change is the way we look back on the road travelled.
p.5: The years gone by can be seen with more distance. What was lived together can appear in a new light.
p.6:
The family story doesn’t disappear.

It can become a resource.
p.7: Receiving a story doesn’t mean having to repeat it. It means being able to recognise what was passed on, to understand what helped shape a person… and to stay free to invent what comes next.

1.quote: A story received can become something to lean on without becoming an imposed path.

2.intro:
At eighteen, psychological, emotional, relational and material independence naturally keeps on growing.

For those who have walked alongside the child, something changes too: it is no longer only about protecting, guiding or passing on, but gradually about recognising a young adult able to make their own choices.

Societies have always sought to give this passage a symbolic form. Rites made it possible to recognise that a child was gradually taking on a new responsibility and a different place in the community.

Carnet de Vie follows this idea in its own way: making a story visible so that it can be recognised without confining anyone.
2.quote: Recognising the road travelled also means setting free the one who will keep writing it.

4.title: The threshold message

p.1:
Eighteen perhaps deserves something more than a simple “happy birthday”.

Not necessarily a grand speech.

Just a few words that acknowledge the passage.
p.2: Anyone who wishes to — parent, grandparent, brother, sister, family member, godparent, friend or loved one — can leave a personal message.
p.3:
One question can guide this testimony:

“When I look at you today, at 18, what do I especially recognise in you, and what would I like to wish you for what comes next?”
p.4: It might be a quality noticed since childhood, a shared memory, a change that is especially moving, a strength discovered over the years, or simply a few words for the future.
p.5:
There is no need to give advice.

There is no need to say what the young adult should become.

It is simply about bearing witness to what is seen and felt today.

4.quote: Recognising someone also means leaving them free to become other than what we imagine.
4.invite: We invite anyone who wishes to keep a trace of this passage to leave their message, written, audio or video, in Carnet de Vie. One day, the young adult will be able to rediscover how they were seen at the time they turned 18.

p.1: In many societies, moving from one age or status to another has been marked by rites.
p.2: The source document recalls several religious or cultural forms: Bar or Bat Mitzvah in Judaism, confirmation in Christianity, Upanayana in some Hindu traditions, as well as various forms of initiation or temporary withdrawal from the community in traditional societies.
p.3: The forms are extremely different, but a shared purpose appears: making a passage visible.
p.4: Arnold van Gennep (1873–1957) – French ethnologist and folklorist.
p.5: Van Gennep devoted his work to rites of passage, which accompany life’s great transitions and allow a change of status to be recognised symbolically. The source document draws on this very idea to think about the passage into adulthood.
p.6: Joseph Campbell (1904–1987) – American professor of literature and specialist in comparative mythology.
p.7: The source document links Campbell to the stories in which the passage from childhood to independence takes the form of a symbolic journey.
p.8: In today’s societies, the markers of entry into adulthood are often more blurred.
p.9: The 18th birthday can then become a symbolic moment: not to declare that a person is suddenly “complete”, but to recognise the road travelled and the new place that is starting to take shape.
p.10: Carnet de Vie can be part of this passage by giving concrete form to a story until now scattered across memories, images, voices and tales.

points.1: Societies have often marked life’s great transitions with rites.
points.2: A rite makes a change of place or status visible.
points.3: Eighteen can be a symbolic threshold without meaning that development is over.
points.4: Recognising the passage doesn’t mean imposing a direction for what comes next.
points.5: Carnet de Vie can give this recognition a contemporary, family form.

histoire.title: Receiving one’s story without having to repeat it

p.1: A family story passes on much more than memories.
p.2: It passes on values, ways of loving, habits, stories, beliefs, silences, strengths and sometimes vulnerabilities.
p.3: But receiving doesn’t mean having to repeat.
p.4: The source document states this intention very clearly: Carnet de Vie seeks to make a story visible so that it can be received without confining anyone. The aim is to offer something to lean on, from which the young adult can carry on along their own path.
p.5: At eighteen, this distinction becomes especially important.
p.6:
The young adult can recognise what they were given and, gradually, decide:

what they want to keep,

what they want to transform,

what they want to understand differently,

and sometimes what they want to leave behind.
p.7: This takes nothing away from those who passed it on.
p.8: On the contrary, a fully living transmission accepts being transformed by the one who receives it.
p.9:
So Carnet de Vie doesn’t say:

“This is who you are.”

Rather, it says:

“Here is part of your story as those who walked alongside you lived it and saw it. Now it’s up to you to carry on along your path.”

points.1: A family story can be a resource without becoming an obligation.
points.2: Passing on doesn’t mean asking the young adult to repeat the choices or values of those who came before.
points.3: Some things passed on will be kept, others questioned or transformed.
points.4: Accepting this transformation is part of the process of passing on.
points.5: Carnet de Vie offers a story and traces; it doesn’t define the identity of the one who receives them.

closing.1: Growing up means making peace with one’s story in order to move forward.
